entities.name: Franciscus Accursius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Franciscus Accursius (c. 1225–1293) emerged as a prominent Italian jurist and professor of civil law during the High Middle Ages, a period characterized by the rediscovery and systematic study of Roman law. As the son of the vastly influential glossator Accursius, author of the *Glossa Ordinaria*, Franciscus navigated a scholarly landscape dominated by his father's legacy, contributing to the ongoing development of legal scholarship at the University of Bologna. His career spanned a critical juncture when Roman legal principles were being reinterpreted and integrated into European jurisprudence, laying foundations for modern legal systems.

After studying law at Bologna, Franciscus Accursius succeeded his father as a professor, continuing the tradition of glossing and commenting on Justinian's *Corpus Juris Civilis*. His academic renown extended beyond Italy, leading to a significant invitation from King Edward I of England in 1273. Franciscus taught Roman law at the nascent University of Oxford for several years, from approximately 1273 to 1275 or 1280, and served as a legal advisor to the English monarch. This period marked a rare and direct transmission of Italian civilian legal thought into England, a country where common law traditions were predominantly shaping the legal framework.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Franciscus Accursius played a significant role in the transmission of advanced Roman legal thought from Italy to England, briefly influencing the nascent common law tradition and the court of Edward I. His work contributed to the broader European integration of legal scholarship during the High Middle Ages.
